summary: This memo specifies a Telnet option for passing environment information, such as variable settings, from a client to a server. It is historic.

eli5.summary: When you log into a faraway computer, it sometimes helps for it to know settings from your own. This paper explains how to pass those settings along. It is historic.

questions: what is the telnet environment option
how does telnet send environment variables
subtitle: A Telnet option that lets a client pass environment variables such as USER and DISPLAY to the server at login.

tldr.problem: Operating systems keep startup information and environment variables that a remote host could use, but adding a new Telnet option for each new piece of information would not scale.
tldr.mechanism: The ENVIRON option (option 36) lets the side that sent DO ask for variables with SEND, and the side that sent WILL answer with IS, carrying typed VAR or USERVAR names and VALUE entries.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is marked Historic and was later updated by RFC 1571.

today: RFC 1408 is marked Historic, and the unit metadata lists RFC 1571 as updating it. Treat it as a record of how the option was first specified rather than as a current definition.

sections.title: Why a Generic Environment Option
sections.content:
Many operating systems have startup information and environment variables that should be passed to a remote machine when a Telnet connection is set up. Instead of defining a new Telnet option every time someone needs some new piece of information carried along, RFC 1408 defines one generic option for it.

The Telnet session itself does not need to understand the information. It only carries it. The default is WONT ENVIRON and DONT ENVIRON, which means no environment information is exchanged unless both sides agree.
sections.eli5: Instead of making a new form for every little thing, there is one big blank form where you can write any setting you want to share.

sections.title: Commands and Codes
sections.content:
The option is called ENVIRON and has the code 36. Inside a subnegotiation there are three commands: IS (0), SEND (1) and INFO (2). Variable entries use the type markers VAR (0), VALUE (1), ESC (2) and USERVAR (3).

The side that sent DO ENVIRON may send a SEND request, optionally naming the variables it wants. With no list, the default environment of both well known and user defined variables should be sent. Only the side that sent WILL ENVIRON may answer with IS, and it must reply in the same order as the request and give a response for each variable explicitly requested.

A variable name follows a VAR or USERVAR marker, and its value follows a VALUE marker. A name with no value is undefined, while a VALUE followed directly by another marker means the variable is defined but empty. If a name or value contains IAC, it is sent as IAC IAC. If it contains VAR, USERVAR, VALUE or ESC, it is preceded by ESC.

INFO looks like IS but carries changes to variables. It is not used for initial information, and may be sent spontaneously by the WILL side.
sections.eli5: There are a few special words: one to ask, one to answer, and one to say something changed. Little markers show where each name and each value starts.

sections.title: Well Known Variables
sections.content:
Six variables are well known: USER (the account name to log into), JOB (a job ID), ACCT (an account ID), PRINTER (the default printer output location, whose format is left undefined), SYSTEMTYPE (the operating system type, matching the FTP SYSTEM command value) and DISPLAY (the X display location, written <host>:<dispnum>[.<screennum>]).

If both DISPLAY and the Telnet X-DISPLAY-LOCATION option arrive and disagree, the most recently received information should be used. For anything else, the USERVAR type lets users send arbitrary name and value pairs. It helps a server tell values derived by host software apart from values the user supplied, though the RFC notes that paranoid implementations will probably distrust both equally.
sections.eli5: Some settings have agreed names, like your user name and which screen to draw on. For anything else you can invent your own name.

sections.title: How the Exchange Runs
sections.content:
WILL and DO are used only at the start of the connection, to grant permission. Once they are exchanged, the DO side may request variables. The option may be used at any time, but the exchange usually happens at startup, because many operating systems only pass environment information when a process is created, before the user logs in.

The receiving host does not have to put every variable into the environment. If the terminal type was already learned through the TERMINAL-TYPE option, it can ignore a TERM value. It may also use USER, ACCT and PROJ to choose an account without ever storing them. The suggested approach is to put all unknown information into the user's environment, since that gives the user the most flexibility.

An empty IS reply is legal when no variables are defined. Anyone who supports the option is expected to support all of this specification.
sections.eli5: The two computers first agree to talk about settings. Then one asks and the other answers, usually right at the start, and the receiver is free to ignore what it does not need.

sections.title: Security Concerns
sections.content:
The RFC warns implementors to think about how setting variables interacts with login and authentication. They should analyze carefully which variables are safe to set before the client has logged in.

The example of a bad choice is allowing a variable to be changed in a way that lets an intruder get around or compromise the login or authentication program itself.
sections.eli5: If a stranger can change your settings before showing who they are, they might trick the door guard. So be careful about which settings you accept early.

messages.label: IAC DO ENVIRON
messages.note: Host1 is willing to receive variables.

messages.label: IAC WILL ENVIRON
messages.note: Host2 is willing to send them.

messages.label: IAC SB ENVIRON SEND VAR "USER" VAR "ACCT" VAR USERVAR IAC SE
messages.note: Asks for USER, ACCT and the default sets.

messages.label: IAC SB ENVIRON IS VAR "USER" VALUE "joe" ... IAC SE
messages.note: Returns the variables with their values.
